title: Tenant Throttle Siphon and Resilience Proposal
content:
Context:
Redwood Dedicated customers expect both predictable reserved throughput and the flexibility to absorb short-lived spikes. Existing reserve + burst designs focus on hard credit buckets, preemption, and soft-eviction. We still see two recurring risks in customer incidents and internal load tests: (1) fast, small-duration microbursts that trigger expensive cold-warm cycle churn, and (2) noisy-tenant patterns that slowly erode pool headroom and cause tail-latency regressions for other tenants.

Problem statement:
- Need an autoscaling and overflow mechanism that reduces cold-start churn while preserving reservoir headroom for SLAs.
- Need a tenant-level shaping layer that can continuously attenuate noisy traffic patterns while keeping SLA guarantees stable for paying customers.
- Operations needs a principled way to route transient demand to opportunistic capacity without risky preemptions or surprise evictions.

Product goal (one-liner):
Introduce a tenant siphon model (transient attenuation + opportunistic spill) that smooths bursts, limits noisy neighbor impact, and gives predictable fallbacks for Dedicated customers.

Success criteria (90 days after GA):
- P99 serving latency for reserved lane customers remains within 10% of baseline under bursty workloads.
- 30% reduction in cold-warm GPU spin-ups observed in synthetic microburst tests.
- <2% increase in mean cost-per-token for reserved customers while overall system cost decreases in high-variance scenarios.
- No unplanned evictions during canary (see rollout).

Non-goals:
- This does not change contract-level guarantees for Reserved plans (we must still honor committed capacity); siphon is a protective, not a replacement, mechanism.
- Not addressing model packing or kernel-level optimizations (runtime team handles that).

Design overview (high level):
1) Transient attenuation (siphon layer):
   - For incoming requests to a dedicated tenant, add a short-lived fast path that measures instantaneous request rate and a burst-shape factor (exponential moving average over 5s).
   - When rate exceeds configured burst threshold, divert a fraction of requests (configurable by tier) into a siphon lane: these requests are (a) queued into a short delay buffer (10–200ms) to allow natural smoothing, and (b) if delay exceeds a threshold, routed to opportunistic capacity or downgraded via cheaper quantized model.
   - Siphon lanes are allowed to use cached KV-prefetch and prefix coalescing aggressively to minimize per-token cost.

2) Opportunistic spill pool (shared ephemeral capacity):
   - Pool made of pre-warmed ephemeral workers (lower-priority VMs/GPU) with constrained concurrency and shorter prewarm windows.
   - Allocation uses credit-weighted fair-share: tenants that paid for burst credits or have underused reserved capacity get priority for spill.
   - Spill pool enforces a max-per-tenant consumption cap and a decay window (credits refresh slowly).

3) Priority smoothing and automatic backoff: 
   - When siphon overflow is sustained, we apply a gradual attenuation curve to the tenant's request admission (e.g., down to 50% acceptance over 60s) rather than an abrupt cutoff.
   - Backoff parameters are influenced by tier, SLA, and historical noisiness score. Noisy tenants get steeper attenuation.

4) Isolation controls and noisy neighbor detection:
   - Add a runtime noisiness score per tenant using features: request variance, mean tokens per request, KV cache miss-rate, QPS-to-reserved-capacity ratio, and error rate spikes.
   - Score feeds into: (a) attenuation severity, (b) eligibility for spill pool, (c) operator alerts.

5) Safe preemption and canary fallback:
   - If opportunistic capacity is exhausted, requests fallback to: (a) compatible model variant with lower compute (quantized faster model), (b) degrade features (no streaming / truncated outputs), or (c) best-effort queuing with client-visible retry guidance.

Config surface:
- Tenant config: burst_threshold_qps, burst_window_s, max_siphon_fraction, burst_credit_balance_id, attenuation_curve_id, noisy_tenant_ttl_days.
- Global knobs: spill_pool_size, spill_pool_min_prewarm, opportunistic_priority_policy.
- UI/Console: new "Burst & Siphon" pane showing real-time siphon utilization, credit burn, noisy score, and historical smoothing events.

API/SDK changes (developer UX):
- New optional header in request: X-Redwood-Burst-Hint: {expected_workload:"spiky"|"steady", max_wait_ms: 150} so client can indicate tolerance for queuing or degradation.
- Admin API for tenants to view and buy burst credits, and to opt-in to fallback models.

Operational & telemetry:
- New metrics: tenant_siphon_accept_rate, tenant_siphon_queue_ms_p50/95/99, tenant_noisy_score, spill_pool_consumption, siphon_fallback_count.
- Alerts: sustained tenant_noisy_score > threshold for 10m; spill_pool_utilization > 90% for 5m.
- Add replayable simulator to simulate tenant mixtures (50 tenants, 10 noisy, 5 microbursters) and produce expected tail-latency / cost impact.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (internal): run simulator + synthetic load tests (2 weeks).
- Phase 1 (alpha): opt-in for internal product tenants + two pilot customers. Observe for 4 weeks. Keep siphon default very conservative (max_siphon_fraction 0.1).
- Phase 2 (beta): enable on 10% of production Enterprise tenants with detailed dashboards and runbook. Test spill pool scaling rules.
- Phase 3 (GA): enable for all Dedicated customers with conservative defaults, allow admin opt-out.

Risk & mitigations:
- Risk: Over-aggressive attenuation causes customer UX regressions. Mitigation: slow ramping, observability, easy opt-out, visible client headers to communicate degradation.
- Risk: Spill pool costs spiral with many simultaneous microbursts. Mitigation: hard caps, decay-based credit accounting, and automated scale-in thresholds tied to overall spend targets.
- Risk: Gaming the system by sending many small cheap requests to exploit siphon caching. Mitigation: noisiness features include token distribution and cache miss signals; adapt cost to discourage abuse.

SRE runbook excerpt (short):
- If tenant_siphon_queue_ms_p99 > 2s and reserved P99 latency degraded: (1) throttle siphon by lowering max_siphon_fraction to 0.05 for tenant, (2) increase spill_pool_min_prewarm by +10% for 15m, (3) notify engineering.
- If spill_pool_utilization stays >95% for 10m: scale down spill eligibility (only paid burst credits) and open incident.

Open questions / design tradeoffs:
- How to price burst credits while keeping incentives aligned? (flat monthly allotment vs on-demand credits).
- Should noisy_score be visible to customers or only operators? Visibility helps remediation but may be gamed.
- How tightly should siphon lane be tied to model-awareness (some models compress better)?

Experiments to run quickly:
- Microburst flapping test: 100x 200ms bursts at random alignment with 500ms gaps; measure GPU spin-ups and tail latency.
- Mixed-tenancy headroom erosion: 30 tenants with one noisy tenant ramping qps slowly; measure tail-latency and cost.
- Cost vs UX tradeoff sweep: vary max_siphon_fraction and spill_pool_size and measure delta in cost-per-token vs P99.

Next steps (owners):
- Product: finalize UI fields and org-wide defaults (owner: Asha Patel).
- Infra: prototype siphon lane buffer and opportunistic spill allocator (owner: Marcus Lee).
- Applied ML: recommend fallback model candidates and quantization thresholds (owner: Sofia Nguyen).
- SRE: add telemetry gaps and runbook draft (owner: Diego Alvarez).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative: objective is to reduce churn and smooth tails rather than maximize burst absorption. Please call out any edge cases where reserved-contracted customers may be negatively impacted.

References and linked docs:
- See linked artifacts at top for simulator and initial benchmark PR.
